PMGT1852 Week 12

PMGT1852 Week 12 - The Secrets to Information Gathering: Knowing the Tools and How to Use Them

Overview

A facilitated session earns its value by involving people in meaningful work, not by presenting at them. This week covers:

• Why the way participants engage must vary from item to item.

• The seven building-block information-handling functions.

• Modes (full group, breakout groups, pairs, individual) and orders (random, round-robin, assigned).

• Gathering facts: ask, record, react.

• Categorising: one item at a time, asking "Same or different?".

• Inquiring: pre-questioning for a question-and-answer session.

• Generating ideas (brainstorming): ask, record, but do not react.

• Prioritising: define criteria, permit lobbying, check for consensus after scoring.

• Reporting back: appointing primary commenters.

• Getting feedback: strengths, ways to improve, and the degree of consensus behind each comment (rated feedback).

Key Concepts

Why vary engagement

If information only needs to be presented, it can usually be provided in writing. In a facilitated session, every process must put participants into a meaningful activity: without participation the audience gets little value. Most presentations involve the audience only in the final question time.

Building-block processes

The seven functions below are building blocks. They can be combined to reach higher-level goals such as issue resolution, team building and strategic planning.

Reacting questions

Reacting questions are the facilitator's responses during a discussion. They are used to acknowledge, clarify, challenge, confirm, probe and redirect.

A score is not a decision

A score is only a score. After any scoring activity, check for consensus before treating the ranking as a decision.

Frameworks and Formulas

The seven building-block functions

Function

Sample question

Purpose

Gathering facts

How does the process work today?

Get detailed information; best when there is a "right" answer

Categorising

What are the key groupings represented by this information?

Group information so it can be processed further

Inquiring

What questions do we want to see answered?

Participants raise questions, or question a speaker, a group member or each other

Generating ideas

What are possible ways this problem could be solved?

Produce possible solutions; best when many answers are possible and creativity is needed

Prioritising

Which of these solutions is best?

Rank, rate or select

Reporting

What did your group come up with?

Report the results of a breakout or other activity

Getting feedback

What were the strengths and weaknesses of today's session?

Evaluate the session or another experience

Modes and orders

Mode

When to use it

Full group

Everyone must hear the same information at the same time, or each person knows only part of the picture

Breakout groups

A process must be run several times

Pairs

Denser one-to-one interaction or team building is needed

Individual

Reflection or introspection, usually before breaking out and sharing with the large group

Order

When to use it

Random

The sequence does not matter; call on people by name

Round-robin

Everyone needs a turn to contribute

Assigned order

The task has been sequenced in advance

Prioritising: methods and criteria

The secret of prioritising: define criteria; permit lobbying; check for consensus after scoring.

Methods:

• Dot method - each participant receives a limited number of dots (votes); the items with the most dots come first.

• Weighted score - each criterion has a weight x; each participant rates each strategy on that criterion with a rating y; the weighted score for that criterion is x times y. Adding the weighted scores of all criteria gives the strategy's total score, and the totals set the ranking.

• Hybrid - dots combined with a high-medium-low rating scale.

Minimum criteria:

• Impact - the effect on the key objectives if the strategy is implemented successfully.

• Probability of success - how likely it is that the strategy will succeed.

• Cost-effectiveness - tangible and intangible outcomes compared with cost and resources.

Lobbying period before the vote: everyone may explain why a strategy deserves support. This gives equal opportunity to express opinions and exert influence, it builds consensus (for example around strategies that are repeatedly argued for), and people who lobby for a winning strategy feel more committed to implementing it.

Worked Examples

Gathering facts: ask, record, react (hiring steps)

Title the flip chart.

Describe the activity and its purpose - a checkpoint covering what has been done, what comes next and why it matters.

Give the general directions in the six-part instruction format (purpose, example, directions, exceptions, questions, starting question).

Ask a Type B starting question: "Think about the last time you hired someone ... the hurdles you had to jump over. Let's build a list. Sandra, get me started ..."

Capture the participants' own words immediately and legibly (write first, discuss second; write what they said).

Respond with reacting questions - acknowledge, clarify, challenge, confirm, probe, redirect: "Why is that important?", "It sounds like what you are saying is ... Is that right?", "Are there steps related to ...?", "Is this related to that comment? OK to combine them?"

Keep going with prompt and extended prompt questions: "What else?"

Categorising: one item at a time, "Same or different?"

Lay out all the items so they can be seen.

Describe the activity and its purpose (expect roughly 3-8 categories).

Give directions: go item by item; create a new category when needed; review at the end.

Read the first item and let the group name its category (the facilitator may suggest a name such as "Announcement" for "HR places ad in paper", but confirms agreement).

Write the item under its category heading.

For the next item ask: "Should this go into the previous group(s), or is it different?"

Repeat until every item is placed (tip: let the groups take turns naming, or assign categories to groups).

Review the finished groupings - for example Announcement, Screening and Acceptance - and ask whether a small category should be merged into another or kept; the group decides (for example keep "Acceptance" and add the item "Candidate negotiates offer").

Inquiring: pre-questioning for a question-and-answer session

Scenario: the sponsor has brought in a hiring expert for the agenda item "What are the potential improvements?".

Describe the activity and its purpose: find the most important questions before hearing the expert, which also tells the speaker what matters most to the group.

Split into breakout teams.

Give directions: 2 minutes, one question per sticky note; when time is called, pens capped and notes held in the air.

Ask the starting question.

Group the sticky notes with the categorising technique (for example A Technology, B Timing).

Checkpoint, hand the questions to the speaker, and say clearly that not all questions will be answered.

After the talk, give 3 minutes (with a new team leader in each group) to review the assigned category, remove the questions already answered, and select up to three questions to ask the speaker.

Allow up to 4 minutes of questions per group, with "permission to be rude": interrupt once a question has been answered well enough.

Give 3 more minutes to review the remaining questions and mark how each should be handled - a team meeting, assigned to a person, or dropped. Collect them for the meeting record.

Generating ideas: ask, record, but do not react

Describe the activity and its purpose.

Set a time limit and give the directions - for example 5 minutes, round the room starting with Joe, one idea each in verb-object form ("Implement this; develop that"); say "pass" if stuck; expect four or more rounds.

Prohibit judgement of any kind: "If you think 'That won't work', ask yourself 'What will work? How can I improve on it?'"

Ask a Type B starting question.

Write the ideas down exactly as stated.

Use prompt and extended prompt questions.

Ask for last thoughts: "Any last-minute ideas?"

Follow with a grouping or prioritising activity.

Contrast with gathering facts: there the facilitator reacts to answers; in brainstorming the facilitator does not react, because any reaction judges the ideas.

Reporting back: appointing primary commenters

Scenario: five breakout teams, each developing an action plan for one of five priority strategies.

Describe the activity and its purpose, then give the directions: each group has 4 minutes and must cover at least the action steps, responsibilities and timeline; one other group is appointed as the primary commenters, who comment first - saying what they like first, then how to improve - and then the other groups join in. The commenting groups are told their task in advance.

After the primary team gives strengths and improvement suggestions and the floor is opened, all suggestions are captured. Each suggestion is then confirmed with the group (for example by simple majority, since these are recommendations), and the group decides whether to implement it.

Getting feedback: strengths, ways to improve, rated feedback

Scenario: the last agenda item, "Review and close", after reviewing the steps, decisions, issues and actions. Process feedback supports the facilitator's continuing development; rated feedback produces both high-quality comments and a measure of how much support each comment has. (Begin with the activity purpose and the directions, as always.)

Strengths first - round-robin, starting with Jamie, one item each. "Ditto number one" adds a tick to an item already named.

Ways to improve - in random order, and worded as "ways to improve" rather than "what are the weaknesses": "If we had a chance to do this all over again, what would you do differently?"

Test the support for each improvement suggestion with a show of hands (for example "about 80 percent").
